PART A
```{r}
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m1
```

```{r}
m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2
```

```{r}
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
scores
```

Question #1
- With byrow = TRUE, it places the values across the first row from left to right, then continues on to the next row.

Question #2
```{r}
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
```
- Once it gets to 8, it returns to 1 because it runs out of values. It also gives a warning that the data length is not a multiple of the number of rows.


Question #3
```{r}
class(scores[1, ])
class(scores[, "Ben"])
```
-R reduces a single row or column to a plain numeric vector. Since one row or column only has one dimension, R removes the extra dimension it doesn’t need.

Question #4
-A logical condition returns the individual elements where the condition is true. R returns a plain vector in column major order.

Question #5
-Element-wise multiplication works on matching positions, while matrix multiplication relies on linear algebra operations.

Question #6
-Row names label the rows and column names label the columns. When a matrix is transposed, rows become columns and columns become rows, so the names must swap too, otherwise each label would point to the wrong values.

PART D

```{r}
scores_v2
```
```{r}
scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3
```

Question #7
-R gives a warning and cuts the vector down, keeping only the first 2 values (85, 91) and leaving out the 100.

Question #8
-rbind() is the right choice when each new batch of data is a new observation that uses the same variables.

Question #9
-dim(arr) gives 2 3 2, where the first number (2) is how many rows each layer has, the second (3) is how many columns each layer has, and the third (2) is how many layers are stacked together.

Question #10
-A real-world example is product demand, where the rows are months, the columns are locations, and the third dimension is the product category. A 2D matrix can only hold two variables at once, so the data would have to be merged and flattened to fit.

PART F
```{r}
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                   dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students
```
```{r}
rowMeans(all_students)
```

Question #11
-I chose rbind() because both matrices have the same column names (Midterm and Final). When the variables match across matrices, rbind() is the right function to stack them together.

Question #12
-The best approach is to stack all 5 matrices on top of each other using row binding. After that, I would run dim() on the result to confirm it still has 2 columns and that the number of rows equals the total number of students across all the classes.

CONCLUSION
-A matrix is a two-dimensional structure (rows and columns), while an array can have three or more dimensions, such as rows, columns, and layers. Both hold a single data type. In an attendance monitoring dataset where each row is a week and each column is a student, cbind() can add a new student as a new column, and rbind() can add a new week as a new row. This lets you keep growing the dataset without rebuilding the matrix from scratch.
